web-api-1.pitch: In my experience, ASP.NET Web API is the backbone of any modern .NET service layer. At my previous role I used it to build REST APIs consumed by React SPAs and mobile clients — the clean HTTP verb mapping and built-in JSON serialization meant we could ship a new endpoint in minutes, not hours. It is my default choice any time a client needs to talk to a .NET backend over HTTP.
web-api-1.definition: ASP.NET Web API is a framework for building HTTP-based RESTful services on top of the .NET platform. It maps HTTP verbs — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE — directly to controller action methods, making it natural to design resource-oriented APIs. Unlike ASP.NET MVC, which renders HTML views for browsers, Web API returns raw data (JSON or XML) intended for programmatic consumption by any client. ASP.NET Core Web API is the modern, cross-platform successor running on .NET 5+ with improved performance and middleware pipeline.
advantages: Full REST support — HTTP verbs map directly to actions, making API design intuitive and standard
Content negotiation — automatically returns JSON or XML based on the client's Accept header with no extra code
Lightweight and fast — no SOAP envelope, no complex WCF config, just plain HTTP
First-class DI, middleware, and filter pipeline integration in ASP.NET Core
disadvantages: Not suitable for real-time bidirectional communication — use SignalR or WebSockets for chat or live updates
No built-in support for reliable messaging, transactions, or advanced WS-* standards that WCF offers
similarQuestions: What is the difference between ASP.NET Web API and ASP.NET MVC?
When would you choose gRPC over ASP.NET Core Web API?

diagram.title: ASP.NET Web API request flow
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Client] -->|HTTP Request| B[Routing]
  B --> C[Controller / Action]
  C --> D[Business Logic]
  D --> E[(Database)]
  C -->|JSON Response| A

web-api-1.why: It is used because it gives a lightweight, standards-based way to expose application logic and data over HTTP, so any client (browsers, mobile apps, other services) can consume it regardless of platform or language. Teams pick it for its clean REST conventions, automatic content negotiation (JSON/XML), built-in model binding and validation, and tight integration with the .NET ecosystem such as dependency injection, middleware, and authentication. That cuts boilerplate and lets developers ship and evolve scalable, testable APIs quickly.

web-api-2.pitch: ASP.NET Web API builds HTTP services that return data; ASP.NET MVC builds web apps that return HTML views; ASP.NET Core Web API is the modern, cross-platform, high-performance successor that unifies both on .NET 5+.
web-api-2.definition: ASP.NET Web API builds HTTP services that return data; ASP.NET MVC builds web apps that return HTML views; ASP.NET Core Web API is the modern, cross-platform, high-performance successor that unifies both on .NET 5+.
advantages: Web API is purpose-built for REST/JSON services consumed by SPAs, mobile and other services.
MVC is ideal when the server renders HTML pages directly for browsers.
ASP.NET Core merges MVC and Web API into one framework and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS.
disadvantages: Classic Web API and MVC are Windows/.NET Framework only and slower than Core.
Mixing view-rendering and API concerns in old MVC could blur responsibilities.
Migrating legacy Web API/MVC to ASP.NET Core needs code and hosting changes.

web-api-3.pitch: Web API is a lightweight framework for RESTful HTTP services using simple verbs and JSON; WCF is a heavier framework for building services across many protocols (HTTP, TCP, named pipes, MSMQ) with SOAP and contracts.
web-api-3.definition: Web API is a lightweight framework for RESTful HTTP services using simple verbs and JSON; WCF is a heavier framework for building services across many protocols (HTTP, TCP, named pipes, MSMQ) with SOAP and contracts.
advantages: Web API is simpler, REST-first and a natural fit for the open web and mobile.
Web API uses plain HTTP and JSON, so any client can consume it with no SDK.
Web API has less configuration and ceremony than WCF.
disadvantages: WCF supports protocols and features (transactions, message queuing) Web API does not.
WCF is better for intranet, duplex or non-HTTP transport scenarios.
WCF's contracts and bindings add complexity that REST avoids.

web-api-4.pitch: Choose ASP.NET Web API when you need a RESTful, HTTP/JSON service for browsers, mobile apps or public clients, and you do not need WCF's extra transports or SOAP features.
web-api-4.definition: Choose ASP.NET Web API when you need a RESTful, HTTP/JSON service for browsers, mobile apps or public clients, and you do not need WCF's extra transports or SOAP features.
advantages: Best for public, internet-facing REST APIs.
Lightweight and easy for non-.NET clients to call.
Less configuration, faster to ship.
disadvantages: Not ideal when you need TCP, named pipes or MSMQ.
No built-in SOAP, WS-* or distributed transactions.
Duplex/callback messaging is not a natural fit.
web-api-4.when: Pick Web API for HTTP/REST services on the open web, mobile back ends, microservices and any case where clients are diverse and you want plain JSON over HTTP. Choose WCF only when you specifically need non-HTTP transports, SOAP/WS-* standards, or message-queue style communication.

web-api-5.pitch: The Web API request lifecycle is the ordered set of stages a request passes through: hosting, routing, controller selection, model binding, filters, the action method, the result/formatter, and finally the HTTP response.
web-api-5.definition: The Web API request lifecycle is the ordered set of stages a request passes through: hosting, routing, controller selection, model binding, filters, the action method, the result/formatter, and finally the HTTP response.
advantages: A clear pipeline makes behaviour predictable and easy to debug.
Each stage (routing, binding, filters) is an extension point you can customise.
Cross-cutting concerns plug in cleanly via middleware and filters.
disadvantages: Many stages can make tracing a single request harder for beginners.
Misordered middleware or filters can cause subtle bugs.
Custom handlers at the wrong stage can hurt performance.

diagram.title: Web API request lifecycle
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[HTTP Request] --> B[Hosting / Middleware]
  B --> C[Routing]
  C --> D[Controller Selection]
  D --> E[Model Binding]
  E --> F[Filters]
  F --> G[Action Method]
  G --> H[Formatter]
  H --> I[HTTP Response]

web-api-6.pitch: Routing maps an incoming URL and HTTP verb to a specific controller and action, using either attribute routing on the methods or convention-based route templates.
web-api-6.definition: Routing maps an incoming URL and HTTP verb to a specific controller and action, using either attribute routing on the methods or convention-based route templates.
advantages: Attribute routing puts the URL right next to the action for clarity.
Convention routing centralises URL patterns in one place.
Constraints and tokens give fine control over matching.
disadvantages: Overlapping routes can cause ambiguous matches.
Complex route templates become hard to read.
Wrong verb or template often returns a confusing 404/405.

diagram.title: Request routing
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[URL + Verb] --> B[Match Route Template]
  B --> C[Select Controller]
  C --> D[Select Action]
  D --> E[Bind Route Values]

web-api-6.how: The framework parses the request path and method, compares them against registered route templates (for example [HttpGet("products/{id}")]), selects the controller and action whose template and verb match, extracts route values like id, and then hands off to model binding. If two routes match equally it throws an ambiguity error; if none match it returns 404.

web-api-7.pitch: HTTP verbs express the intent of a request: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes, HEAD returns headers only, and OPTIONS reports allowed methods.
web-api-7.definition: HTTP verbs express the intent of a request: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes, HEAD returns headers only, and OPTIONS reports allowed methods.
advantages: Using the right verb makes APIs predictable and RESTful.
Verbs like GET and PUT are safe/idempotent, helping caching and retries.
Clear semantics reduce the need for custom documentation.
disadvantages: Misusing verbs (e.g. GET that changes data) breaks caching and safety.
Some old clients/proxies only support GET and POST.
PATCH semantics (merge vs JSON Patch) can be ambiguous.
web-api-7.when: Use GET to fetch data, POST to create a new resource, PUT to replace a resource fully, PATCH to update a few fields, DELETE to remove it, HEAD to check existence or headers without the body, and OPTIONS for capability/CORS preflight checks.

web-api-8.pitch: HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers that tell the client the outcome of a request: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
web-api-8.definition: HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers that tell the client the outcome of a request: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
advantages: Standard codes let any client understand results without custom logic.
Correct codes enable proper caching, retries and error handling.
They make APIs self-describing and easier to monitor.
disadvantages: Returning 200 for everything hides failures from clients.
Wrong codes (e.g. 500 for bad input) mislead callers and dashboards.
Overusing generic codes loses useful detail.
web-api-8.what: Common codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable.

web-api-9.pitch: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for networked APIs built on resources, identified by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP verbs and representations like JSON.
web-api-9.definition: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for networked APIs built on resources, identified by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP verbs and representations like JSON.
advantages: Stateless requests scale horizontally with ease.
Uniform interface (URLs + verbs) is simple and widely understood.
Cacheable responses improve performance.
disadvantages: Statelessness can mean repeating context (e.g. auth) on every call.
Over- or under-fetching data is common without careful design.
Strict REST can be awkward for actions that are not CRUD.

diagram.title: REST resource interaction
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] -->|GET /products| S[Server]
  S -->|200 + JSON| C
  C -->|POST /products| S
  S -->|201 Created| C

web-api-9.what: Core REST principles: client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, a uniform interface, layered system, and resource-based design with representations.

web-api-10.pitch: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that uses HTTP headers to let a server declare which other origins may call it, relaxing the same-origin policy in a controlled way.
web-api-10.definition: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that uses HTTP headers to let a server declare which other origins may call it, relaxing the same-origin policy in a controlled way.
advantages: Lets trusted front-end apps on other domains call your API safely.
Fine-grained: you allow specific origins, methods and headers.
Handled by standard headers, no client code changes needed.
disadvantages: Misconfiguration (allow all origins) can expose the API.
Preflight (OPTIONS) requests add a round trip.
Only browsers enforce it; it is not a server-side firewall.

diagram.title: CORS preflight
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  B[Browser] -->|OPTIONS preflight| S[Server]
  S -->|Allow-Origin / Methods| B
  B -->|Actual request| S
  S -->|Response| B

web-api-10.how: For a cross-origin call the browser may first send an OPTIONS preflight asking which methods/headers are allowed. The server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers. If the actual origin and method are permitted, the browser then sends the real request and exposes the response; otherwise it blocks the response.

web-api-11.pitch: You enable CORS in ASP.NET Core by registering a CORS policy in services and applying it with UseCors in the middleware pipeline, specifying allowed origins, methods and headers.
web-api-11.definition: You enable CORS in ASP.NET Core by registering a CORS policy in services and applying it with UseCors in the middleware pipeline, specifying allowed origins, methods and headers.
advantages: Central policy keeps cross-origin rules in one place.
Named policies let different endpoints have different rules.
Works with credentials, headers and methods configuration.
disadvantages: UseCors placed in the wrong order can silently not apply.
AllowAnyOrigin with credentials is disallowed and error-prone.
Too-broad policies weaken security.
web-api-11.how: In Program.cs call builder.Services.AddCors with a policy (for example WithOrigins("https://app.com").AllowAnyHeader().AllowAnyMethod()), then call app.UseCors("PolicyName") before MapControllers. You can also apply policies per endpoint with the [EnableCors] attribute.

web-api-12.pitch: Parameter binding is how Web API fills an action method's parameters from parts of the request: simple types come from the route or query string, complex types come from the request body.
web-api-12.definition: Parameter binding is how Web API fills an action method's parameters from parts of the request: simple types come from the route or query string, complex types come from the request body.
advantages: Automatic mapping removes manual request parsing.
Clear rules: simple types from URL, complex from body.
Attributes like [FromQuery]/[FromBody] override defaults when needed.
disadvantages: Surprising defaults can bind from the wrong source.
Only one [FromBody] parameter is allowed per action.
Type mismatches cause silent nulls or 400s.

web-api-13.pitch: Model binding builds complex objects from multiple request sources (body, route, query, form, headers) and validates them; parameter binding is the broader mechanism that includes mapping simple values too.
web-api-13.definition: Model binding builds complex objects from multiple request sources (body, route, query, form, headers) and validates them; parameter binding is the broader mechanism that includes mapping simple values too.
advantages: Turns raw request data into strongly-typed models automatically.
Integrates with validation via data annotations and ModelState.
Sources can be mixed with [From*] attributes.
disadvantages: Hidden binding sources can introduce security issues (over-posting).
Complex graphs may bind partially and confuse callers.
Misconfigured sources lead to null models.
web-api-13.how: Model binding inspects the action's parameter types, looks at configured value providers (route, query, form, body), matches incoming names to model properties, converts types, populates the object, and records any errors in ModelState. Parameter binding is the umbrella concept; model binding is its complex-type part.

web-api-14.pitch: Content negotiation is the process where the API and client agree on the response format (JSON, XML, etc.) based on the Accept header and the formatters the server supports.
web-api-14.definition: Content negotiation is the process where the API and client agree on the response format (JSON, XML, etc.) based on the Accept header and the formatters the server supports.
advantages: Clients get data in the format they request.
One endpoint can serve multiple media types.
Defaults keep things working when no Accept header is sent.
disadvantages: Supporting many formats adds testing and maintenance.
Unexpected Accept headers can yield 406 Not Acceptable.
Format-specific bugs are easy to miss.

web-api-15.pitch: Media-type formatters are components that serialize a .NET object to a wire format (e.g. JSON) on the way out and deserialize the body into a .NET object on the way in, selected by content negotiation.
web-api-15.definition: Media-type formatters are components that serialize a .NET object to a wire format (e.g. JSON) on the way out and deserialize the body into a .NET object on the way in, selected by content negotiation.
advantages: Pluggable: add custom formatters for new media types.
Cleanly separate serialization from controller logic.
Reused across all controllers automatically.
disadvantages: Custom formatters must handle edge cases and encoding.
Order of formatters affects which one is chosen.
Heavy serialization can be a performance hotspot.
web-api-15.how: On a request, the formatter matching the Content-Type reads the body into an object for model binding. On a response, content negotiation picks a formatter matching the Accept header, which serializes the returned object and sets the Content-Type. You register formatters in MVC options.

web-api-16.pitch: JSON and XML formatters serialize responses to those formats; JSON is the lightweight default for modern APIs, while XML is verbose but still used by some enterprise clients.
web-api-16.definition: JSON and XML formatters serialize responses to those formats; JSON is the lightweight default for modern APIs, while XML is verbose but still used by some enterprise clients.
advantages: JSON is compact, fast and native to JavaScript clients.
XML supports schemas and namespaces for strict contracts.
You can support both and let clients choose.
disadvantages: XML payloads are larger and slower to parse.
Maintaining two formats doubles serialization concerns.
Inconsistent casing/settings cause client breakage.
web-api-16.how: ASP.NET Core uses JSON by default. To control formats, configure AddControllers().AddXmlSerializerFormatters() to add XML, and set JSON options (casing, nulls) via AddJsonOptions. The default response format is driven by content negotiation and the order of registered formatters; you can also force a format with [Produces("application/json")].

web-api-17.pitch: Filters run code at specific points in the pipeline: authentication filters verify identity, authorization filters check permissions, action filters wrap model binding/execution, and exception filters handle unhandled errors.
web-api-17.definition: Filters run code at specific points in the pipeline: authentication filters verify identity, authorization filters check permissions, action filters wrap model binding/execution, and exception filters handle unhandled errors.
advantages: Centralise cross-cutting concerns instead of repeating code.
Each filter type targets the right stage of the pipeline.
Can be applied globally, per controller or per action.
disadvantages: Filter order and scope can be confusing.
Heavy logic in filters affects every request they cover.
Overusing filters hides logic from the action.
web-api-17.what: Authentication filters establish who the caller is; authorization filters decide if they may proceed; action filters run before/after the action (logging, validation); exception filters catch and translate errors into responses.

web-api-18.pitch: The [Authorize] attribute marks controllers or actions as requiring an authenticated (and optionally role- or policy-satisfying) user before the action runs.
web-api-18.definition: The [Authorize] attribute marks controllers or actions as requiring an authenticated (and optionally role- or policy-satisfying) user before the action runs.
advantages: Declarative security right on the endpoint.
Supports roles, policies and authentication schemes.
[AllowAnonymous] easily opens specific endpoints.
disadvantages: Forgetting it leaves endpoints unprotected.
Policy misconfiguration can over- or under-restrict.
Only as strong as the underlying authentication.
web-api-18.how: During authorization, the framework checks the user's ClaimsPrincipal set by authentication. [Authorize] passes if the user is authenticated; [Authorize(Roles="Admin")] or [Authorize(Policy="...")] additionally evaluate roles or policy requirements. If checks fail it returns 401 (not authenticated) or 403 (not allowed).

web-api-19.pitch: Basic Authentication sends the username and password, Base64-encoded, in the Authorization header on every request.
web-api-19.definition: Basic Authentication sends the username and password, Base64-encoded, in the Authorization header on every request.
advantages: Extremely simple to implement and widely supported.
No extra token infrastructure required.
Useful for quick internal tools or testing.
disadvantages: Credentials travel on every request, only safe over HTTPS.
Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so it is easily decoded.
No expiry or revocation without changing the password.

web-api-20.pitch: JWT bearer authentication issues a signed JSON Web Token after login; the client sends it in the Authorization: Bearer header, and the API validates the signature and claims on each request without server-side session state.
web-api-20.definition: JWT bearer authentication issues a signed JSON Web Token after login; the client sends it in the Authorization: Bearer header, and the API validates the signature and claims on each request without server-side session state.
advantages: Stateless: no server session store needed, scales well.
Self-contained claims carry identity and roles.
Works cleanly across services and domains.
disadvantages: Tokens cannot be easily revoked before expiry.
Large tokens add request overhead.
Leaked tokens grant access until they expire.

diagram.title: JWT authentication flow
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[Client] -->|Login credentials| A[Auth Server]
  A -->|Signed JWT| U
  U -->|Bearer JWT| P[Protected API]
  P -->|Validate signature + claims| P
  P -->|200 + data| U

web-api-21.pitch: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework defining how clients obtain access tokens from an authorization server; JWT is just a token format. OAuth often issues JWTs, but they solve different problems.
web-api-21.definition: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework defining how clients obtain access tokens from an authorization server; JWT is just a token format. OAuth often issues JWTs, but they solve different problems.
advantages: OAuth standardises delegated access and consent flows.
Separates the auth server from the resource API.
Supports third-party login without sharing passwords.
disadvantages: OAuth flows are more complex to set up than plain JWT.
Requires an authorization server / identity provider.
Misimplemented flows can introduce security holes.
web-api-21.how: OAuth 2.0 defines flows (authorization code, client credentials, etc.) where a client gets an access token from an authorization server, then calls the API with it. JWT is one common format for that access token. So JWT is the 'what' (token shape) and OAuth is the 'how' (the protocol to obtain and use it).

web-api-22.pitch: API versioning lets an API evolve without breaking existing clients; common approaches are URL path (/v1/), query string (?api-version=1), header, and media-type (content negotiation) versioning.
web-api-22.definition: API versioning lets an API evolve without breaking existing clients; common approaches are URL path (/v1/), query string (?api-version=1), header, and media-type (content negotiation) versioning.
advantages: Clients can upgrade on their own schedule.
You can deprecate old versions gracefully.
Tooling like Asp.Versioning makes it declarative.
disadvantages: Multiple live versions increase maintenance and testing.
Inconsistent versioning confuses consumers.
Header/media-type versions are less discoverable than URL ones.
web-api-22.why: Versioning matters because public APIs have clients you do not control; a breaking change without a new version would break them. I usually recommend URL-path versioning (/v1/) because it is explicit, easy to test, cache and document, with header versioning as an option when URLs must stay clean.

web-api-23.pitch: Exception handling in Web API converts errors into proper HTTP responses; global exception handling catches unhandled errors in one place (middleware or an exception filter) so every error returns a consistent payload.
web-api-23.definition: Exception handling in Web API converts errors into proper HTTP responses; global exception handling catches unhandled errors in one place (middleware or an exception filter) so every error returns a consistent payload.
advantages: Consistent, safe error responses across the API.
One place to log and format errors.
Hides internal details from clients.
disadvantages: A catch-all can mask specific, recoverable errors.
Poorly designed handlers leak stack traces.
Swallowing exceptions hides real bugs.
web-api-23.how: Add an exception-handling middleware (e.g. app.UseExceptionHandler or a custom IExceptionHandler) early in the pipeline. It wraps the request, catches any unhandled exception, logs it, maps it to a status code (400/404/500), and returns a standard ProblemDetails body. Exception filters can do the same at the MVC layer for controller-specific handling.

web-api-24.pitch: Exception filters handle errors thrown inside the MVC/controller layer and have access to the action context; global exception middleware sits earlier in the pipeline and catches errors from anywhere, including other middleware.
web-api-24.definition: Exception filters handle errors thrown inside the MVC/controller layer and have access to the action context; global exception middleware sits earlier in the pipeline and catches errors from anywhere, including other middleware.
advantages: Filters give controller-aware, fine-grained handling.
Middleware gives one true catch-all for the whole pipeline.
They can be combined: filters for specifics, middleware as backstop.
disadvantages: Filters miss errors that occur outside MVC.
Two layers can duplicate logging if not coordinated.
Ordering matters to avoid double handling.

web-api-25.pitch: Dependency Injection (DI) is a pattern where a class receives its dependencies from an external container instead of creating them; ASP.NET Core has DI built in and uses it throughout the framework.
web-api-25.definition: Dependency Injection (DI) is a pattern where a class receives its dependencies from an external container instead of creating them; ASP.NET Core has DI built in and uses it throughout the framework.
advantages: Loose coupling makes code testable and swappable.
Lifetimes (singleton/scoped/transient) are managed for you.
Promotes clean, single-responsibility classes.
disadvantages: Over-injection leads to bloated constructors.
Wrong lifetimes cause subtle bugs (e.g. captive dependencies).
Indirection can make code harder to follow at first.
web-api-25.why: DI matters because it removes hard-coded 'new' calls, so you can swap implementations (real vs mock), test classes in isolation, and let the framework manage object lifetimes. It is the backbone of clean, maintainable ASP.NET Core apps and is required to plug in services like loggers, DbContexts and HttpClients.

web-api-26.pitch: You secure a Web API by validating and parameterising all input (against SQL injection), encoding output and using tokens/same-site cookies (against XSS and CSRF), enforcing HTTPS and authentication, and following least privilege.
web-api-26.definition: You secure a Web API by validating and parameterising all input (against SQL injection), encoding output and using tokens/same-site cookies (against XSS and CSRF), enforcing HTTPS and authentication, and following least privilege.
advantages: Parameterised queries / ORMs stop SQL injection.
Anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies blunt CSRF.
Validation, encoding and CSP reduce XSS risk.
disadvantages: Security must be applied consistently on every endpoint.
Defenses add complexity and can be misconfigured.
New attack vectors require ongoing review.
web-api-26.how: Use EF Core or parameterised SQL so input is never concatenated (SQL injection); validate and encode all user input and set a Content-Security-Policy (XSS); require anti-forgery tokens or use bearer tokens with SameSite cookies (CSRF); enforce HTTPS, authentication/authorization, rate limiting and least-privilege DB accounts. Keep dependencies patched.

web-api-27.pitch: You improve Web API performance with caching (response and data), response compression, asynchronous (async/await) I/O, pagination and lean payloads, plus connection and query optimisation.
web-api-27.definition: You improve Web API performance with caching (response and data), response compression, asynchronous (async/await) I/O, pagination and lean payloads, plus connection and query optimisation.
advantages: Caching avoids repeating expensive work.
Async frees threads to handle more concurrent requests.
Compression and paging cut payload size and latency.
disadvantages: Caching introduces staleness and invalidation problems.
Async misused (blocking calls) can deadlock or not help.
Aggressive optimisation can complicate the code.
web-api-27.how: Cache hot data (in-memory/distributed) and set HTTP cache headers; enable response compression middleware; make I/O-bound actions async with async/await; page and filter large lists; project only needed columns and add DB indexes; reuse HttpClient and pool connections. Measure with profiling before optimising.

web-api-28.pitch: You document and test Web APIs with Swagger/OpenAPI, which generates an interactive API spec and UI from your code, and with Postman, which lets you craft, save and automate requests.
web-api-28.definition: You document and test Web APIs with Swagger/OpenAPI, which generates an interactive API spec and UI from your code, and with Postman, which lets you craft, save and automate requests.
advantages: Swagger gives live, always-current API docs and a try-it UI.
OpenAPI spec enables client-code generation.
Postman supports saved collections, environments and tests.
disadvantages: Generated docs are only as good as your annotations.
Exposing Swagger in production can leak details.
Manual Postman tests need discipline to stay in sync.
web-api-28.how: Add Swashbuckle/OpenAPI to generate a swagger.json and Swagger UI from your controllers and XML comments; annotate models and responses for richer docs. In Postman, create a collection per API, use environment variables for base URLs and tokens, write test scripts on responses, and run collections in CI with Newman.

web-api-29.pitch: You monitor and troubleshoot production APIs with structured logging, centralised log aggregation, metrics/health checks, and correlation IDs that tie all logs of a single request together across services.
web-api-29.definition: You monitor and troubleshoot production APIs with structured logging, centralised log aggregation, metrics/health checks, and correlation IDs that tie all logs of a single request together across services.
advantages: Structured logs are searchable and machine-friendly.
Correlation IDs trace one request across services.
Metrics and health checks surface problems early.
disadvantages: Too much logging adds noise and cost.
Logging sensitive data is a compliance risk.
Without correlation IDs, distributed tracing is painful.
web-api-29.how: Use a logging framework (Serilog/NLog or built-in ILogger) writing structured JSON to a sink like Seq, ELK or Application Insights. Generate a correlation/trace id per request (or accept an incoming one) and attach it to every log entry and downstream call. Add health-check endpoints, metrics and alerts, and use distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) to follow requests end to end.

web-api-30.pitch: A high-traffic Web API is designed as stateless, horizontally scalable services behind a load balancer, with token-based auth, clear versioning, centralised error handling, caching, async I/O, and an automated deployment pipeline.
web-api-30.definition: A high-traffic Web API is designed as stateless, horizontally scalable services behind a load balancer, with token-based auth, clear versioning, centralised error handling, caching, async I/O, and an automated deployment pipeline.
advantages: Stateless + load balancing scales out under heavy load.
Caching and CDNs absorb read traffic.
CI/CD with health checks enables safe, frequent releases.
disadvantages: More moving parts (cache, gateway, queues) to operate.
Distributed systems need careful consistency and monitoring.
Cost grows with redundancy and scale.

diagram.title: High-traffic API architecture
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Clients] --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> G[API Gateway / Auth]
  G --> S1[API Instance]
  G --> S2[API Instance]
  S1 --> Cache[(Cache)]
  S1 --> DB[(Database)]
  S2 --> Cache
  S2 --> DB
